title: Know When to Hold 'Em. Know When to Fold 'Em.
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: In this Substack piece, education writer Andrew Marcinek argues that AI fluency in classrooms is being taught backwards: students are shown how to prompt, cite, and avoid getting caught using AI, but almost nobody teaches them when a problem is worth outsourcing to a tool versus when the struggle itself is the point of the assignment. Drawing on his own habit of not defaulting to AI or devices in every situation, Marcinek extends the idea to classroom technology generally, arguing that laptops and AI should enter the room 'off' rather than 'on' by default. He cites Manu Kapur's two decades of research on 'productive failure' — students who wrestle with a problem before being shown the solution learn more durably — as the intellectual backbone for protecting struggle in assignments.
points: Argues AI fluency for students isn't about mastering the tool but about judgment: knowing which problems deserve AI and which deserve human struggle.
Criticizes current AI-in-schools instruction for teaching prompting, citing, and avoiding detection while skipping the more important question of 'when.'
Draws on Manu Kapur's research on 'productive failure' to argue some struggle is the point of an assignment, not an obstacle to remove.
Extends the argument beyond AI to all classroom technology: devices should enter the room 'off' by default, not on.
Frames the goal as building students' intentional judgment about tool use, not just their raw technical skill with AI.
quotes: fluency isn't about using the tool well. It's about knowing which problems deserve it — and which ones deserve you.
We've handed students the most powerful tool that's ever entered a classroom, and we're teaching them everything except that.
When is a problem worth taking the tool off the shelf — and when is the struggle the entire point of the assignment?
Technology in our classrooms should enter our classrooms off. The default should never be on.
We want to prepare our students to make intentional, purposeful choices on when it makes sense to grab the laptop and when the problem at hand would benefit from the use of AI.
I don't always need it. Sometimes, in fact, it's more cumbersome to use AI than to just navigate the problem I am working with at the moment.
